name: Emeka Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a cell of computer-controlled milling machines making metal housings for medical pumps. My two-year technical diploma taught me how to set a tool path; on the floor I learned to hear when a cutter is wearing out. I use AI every day to draft setup notes and look up fault codes, then verify the answer against the machine manual and the finished part. I live alone, earn a higher operator rate, have more than six months of expenses saved, and know several plants nearby that need machine people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a modest AI tool can save us time finding a fault code, but it cannot measure a finished housing. I already use it for notes and check the part with a gauge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cell has orders and the work stays mostly physical, so I expect my pay to hold. Savings and nearby plants give me room to test useful tools without making every software update a career decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the milling machines and comparing AI-drafted notes with the manual. In the first year I would ask the junior operator to measure the first housing with me before either of us signs a batch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a little curious. A machine can make a precise part only after somebody notices the cutter has worn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a worn cutter look like in the part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The edge gets a fine burr that catches my glove, and the gauge may still pass the main width. We stop before the whole tray is made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the AI fault answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as a pointer into the manual. A confident answer cannot take responsibility for a medical pump housing that fails inspection.

say: **AI notes** help with faults but cannot measure finished pump housings.
A **gauge check** remains part of batch sign-off.
think: My **operator pay** looks safe in a modest change.
Savings and nearby **plants** give me room to try useful tools.
do: **Keep** setting milling machines and checking AI notes against manuals.
**Measure** the first housing with the junior operator before batch sign-off.
S0.quote: A confident answer cannot take responsibility for a medical pump housing that fails inspection.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is already routine and verified against manuals and parts.
High **pay and savings** make a small change low risk for his own work.

steps.text: Keep setting milling machines and verify AI notes against manuals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the planners that better ordering could spare us late cutters, but the machine cell still needs people to set up and inspect parts. I would volunteer to test a new schedule against actual scrap and downtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI may take more of the buying and planning around my cell, not the cutter changes yet. If the plant cuts setup time on paper, my team could lose paid hours or rush quality checks; I want proof before accepting a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI scheduling screen in a funded paid-time class if an actual place opens, then enter scrap and stoppage data from our last two runs. In the first year I would ask quality control to compare the screen estimate with measured parts before any shorter target is used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a target becoming a wage or quality problem, but keen to see a working system. My scrap tray has a way of correcting optimistic production spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which data would you enter first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cutter change time, the scrap count and the inspection delay on the last pump-housing run. If the planner ignores those, it is not ready for the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a shorter paid setup period?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a supervised run proves the quality checks still fit inside it. I would put the result in writing with quality control so the crew is not blamed for the shortcut.

say: **AI ordering** may prevent late cutters, while operators still set and inspect parts.
A new **schedule** should be tested against scrap and downtime.
think: Shorter **setup time** could cost paid hours or weaken quality.
I want **measured proof** before accepting a production target.
do: **Learn** the AI scheduling screen if a funded paid-time place opens.
**Enter** scrap and stoppage data from two completed runs.
**Compare** targets with quality control before shortening setup time.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour cuts, while interested in testing the new scheduling screen.
S1.quote: My scrap tray has a way of correcting optimistic production spreadsheets.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** concerns an actual scheduling screen, beyond the notes he already drafts daily.
He links **paid time** and quality review to any shorter production target.

steps.text: Take funded AI scheduling class if actual paid-time place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew AGI can plan and buy by 2028, while robots able to change cutters and inspect parts like us follow around 2031. I would get into robot commissioning if the plant opens a paid path before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fully capable robot could remove the setup work that earns my higher operator rate. My savings and the local job market buy time, but other plants may be buying the same machines, so I cannot assume an equal wage elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask engineering for a supervised, paid robot-cell trial and a funded controls course with a real place during paid hours. If I get the place I would complete it; in the first year after 2028 I would apply for a posted local commissioning role only if qualified and its pay and hours cover my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the short route from operator to replaceable operator, even though I like the technology. I want to be the person who can stop a robot before it ruins a tray of medical parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the trial test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safe cutter change, guard interlock and first-part measurement with a technician able to stop the robot. I would want the scrap logged, not hidden in a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If engineering only offers a meeting, do you count that as a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would need a paid slot, a machine isolated for the test and a safety lead present before touching the robot controls.

say: **2028 AGI** changes plans before capable machine robots around 2031.
A paid **robot-cell trial** should test guards and first-part measurement.
think: A robot could remove my **higher setup rate**.
Strong **savings** do not guarantee equal pay at other automated plants.
do: **Complete** funded controls training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local commissioning work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about losing setup work, while interested in controls.
S2.quote: I want to be the person who can stop a robot before it ruins a tray of medical parts.
fieldNote: His **trial request** is conditional on a paid slot, machine isolation and safety lead.
The **commissioning move** requires a real funded course, qualification and posted local bill-covering work.

steps.text: Complete funded robot-controls course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local commissioning role if qualified and pay/hours cover bills
Request paid guarded robot-cell trial with safety lead and technician stop authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets the plant run guarded robot trials and train operators before machines can do all our setup work around 2034. I would help write the first-part inspection rule if quality control lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have time to turn the diploma into a commissioning skill, but only if real machines and experienced engineers are part of the training. A certificate without an opening would not protect my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the milling cell and ask for a paid practical trial with the safety lead. If a funded controls course offers an actual paid-time place, I would finish it; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local commissioning post only if qualified and the base wage and hours cover my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing setup pay around 2034, but not stuck. Five years lets me learn robot commissioning on a guarded milling cell instead of guessing from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the inspection rule say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first robot-made housing gets a gauge check and a visual burr check before the next tray runs. A technician must have the power to stop the cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the commissioning post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its base wage and regular hours with my present shift pay and monthly bills. I would not count uncertain overtime as the difference.

say: **2031 AGI** leaves time for guarded trials before capable robots around 2034.
Quality control needs a **first-part rule** with stop authority.
think: A practical **controls skill** could protect my earnings.
A **certificate** without a real local commissioning opening would not protect my operator wage.
do: **Request** a paid guarded robot trial with the safety lead.
**Finish** funded controls training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local commissioning work if qualified and base pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about setup pay, but able to learn on real equipment.
S3.quote: Five years lets me learn robot commissioning on a guarded milling cell instead of guessing from a video.
fieldNote: He wants **first-part checks** and stop authority written into robot operation.
His **training and application** require a real paid place and a posted local role at adequate base pay.

steps.text: Finish funded robot-controls course if actual paid-time place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell trainees that a decade gives them time to learn both cutter wear and robot controls. AGI might change the plan in 2036, with capable hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be only around forty by the robot date and expect decades more of paid work. If the plant funds practical controls training, I could build a career commissioning machines rather than wait to see whether my current setup job survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the cell and save a fixed fifth of each paid shift bonus starting now. If engineering offers a funded controls course with a real paid-time place, I would complete it before 2039; in the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted local commissioning role only if qualified and its base pay and hours cover my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the long runway, and excited by the work I could learn. The ten-year AGI warning is useful when commissioning training has a real machine attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save from the bonus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bonus varies with output, so a fifth of each paid amount builds new cash without cutting my regular bills. I will not call the savings I already have new saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the plant never funds the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid operator role and ask other nearby plants which real commissioning posts require this diploma. I would not quit for an unfunded course with no job attached.

say: **2036 AGI** changes plans before capable machine robots around 2039.
Trainees can learn **cutter wear** alongside robot controls.
think: I expect **decades of wages** after the robot date.
Practical **commissioning skill** could keep me employed through changes.
do: **Keep** running the milling cell and save a fifth of paid bonuses.
**Complete** funded controls training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local commissioning work if qualified and base pay covers bills.
feel: **Calm** about a long runway and curious about machine work.
S4.quote: The ten-year AGI warning is useful when commissioning training has a real machine attached.
fieldNote: His **early career** and strong savings support a measured move toward commissioning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could reach setup work before I qualify for commissioning. I would need a paid guarded trial, a real funded controls place on paid time and a posted local role at enough base pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The first robot-made pump housing has to pass a gauge and a burr check. Speed is not quality if the tray ends up in the scrap bin.

portrait: **Emeka Mensah**, 27, leads a computer-controlled milling cell making medical pump housings and holds a two-year technical diploma.
He lives **alone**, earns a higher operator rate, has more than six months saved and many nearby factory jobs.
He uses **AI daily** for setup notes and fault codes, verifying against manuals and measured parts.
In the fast scenario he is **anxious** that capable robots could take his setup premium around 2031.
He seeks **funded controls training** and a posted local commissioning role with safe duties and bill-covering base pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives little time before capable robots could remove his higher-paid setup work.
whatWouldHelp: A paid **guarded trial**, real funded course place and posted local commissioning job at adequate base pay would help.
